title: Shortfall as a risk measure: properties, optimization and applications
contribution: Derives shortfall (a mean-adjusted tail conditional expectation) from second-order stochastic dominance, relates it to standard deviation, VaR, lower partial moments and coherent risk, proves it convex, writes the sample mean-shortfall problem as an LP with n+T+1 variables and 2T+2 constraints, and illustrates it on simulated and real portfolios, including cardinality-constrained index tracking as a linear MIP.
problem_entry: {AP+LO; IO, CP, DA precursor} Standard deviation is the industry standard but is exactly right only under quadratic utility or elliptical returns; downside measures are little used for computational reasons and VaR is non-convex and incoherent, so a convex, tractable downside measure is sought (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Shortfall is the criterion whose minimization gives non-dominance for all concave utilities (Levy-Kroll, p. 5). It is proportional to the standard deviation under normal returns, averages VaR below alpha and is convex via the check-function form. Its sample problem is an LP by LP duality for the sum of the K smallest outcomes (pp. 6-10, 15-16).
assumptions: Single-period portfolio with fixed mean and budget; continuous joint returns with finite mean (p. 5). Non-parametric estimator (p. 11), with extreme-value extrapolation for alpha*T < 1 (p. 12). The gradient needs a continuous positive density (p. 10); the Hessian is stated 'Under appropriate conditions' without proof (p. 11); mean-std is an LP only as T grows (p. 17). Data: simulated normal and option-skewed assets, 17 asset classes 1994-2001, 96 S&P 100 stocks 1996-1999 (pp. 18-26).
proof_devices: Theorem 3: the sum of the K smallest components as the LP min{v'z : sum z = K, 0 <= z <= 1} and its dual collapse the exponentially many subset constraints of (19) into the LP (20) with n+T+1 variables and 2T+2 constraints (pp. 15-16)
check-function representation s_alpha(x) = (1/alpha) min_c E[rho_alpha(R'x - c)] gives convexity and the same LP (pp. 9-10, 16)
Levy-Kroll dominance theorem used as the definition of the risk measure (Theorem 1, pp. 4-5)

Theorem 2 / Table 1: optimal VaR and shortfall bounds given mean and standard deviation, attained by distributions, stated without proof via Bertsimas-Popescu 1999; Table 2 model-risk ratio of 3.7 at alpha = 1% (pp. 7-8)
Lagrangean stationarity with the gradient formula (7) for frontier convexity, the riskless-asset ray and shortfall beta (Props. 4-6, pp. 12-14)
normal-model identity between standard deviation and shortfall turns the cardinality-constrained MIQP (26) into the linear MIP (27) (pp. 24-25)
experiments: Simulated normal assets: 100 replications at T = 50/500/2000; the methods agree above alpha ~15%, and shortfall weights are more volatile below (p. 19). Synthetic equal-moment assets skewed by call/put overlays: MV is blind; shortfall dominates in the tails and MV in the mid-range (pp. 20-21). 17 asset classes, in-sample frontiers: MV is slightly better in mean-variance space at alpha = 2.5% (p. 23). S&P 100 index tracking with M = 96 down to 40 stocks via CPLEX (no version, machine or gap), stopped after five feasible solutions: tracking error 0 to 1.1% per month, 0.7-519.3 s (pp. 26-27). No out-of-sample test.
positioning: A variation of mean excess / TailVaR. The body credits the same LP to Uryasev-Rockafellar's CVaR and the gradient, separation and beta results to Tasche (2000) and Scaillet (2000) (pp. 4, 10, 13-16), while the contribution list claims a two-fund separation theorem and a 'new' beta (p. 3). Coherence is handled by re-statement (pp. 8-9).
writing: Five-item contribution list. The abstract is hedged ('might have advantages', p. 1), but the introduction says the shortfall frontier 'outperforms' in mean-standard-deviation space and is 'stable' (p. 4), which the body does not show (pp. 19, 23). A null result is explained by belief (p. 23); the conclusion ends on a conviction (p. 27).
limits_future: Stated: volatile estimates at small alpha (p. 19), extrapolation for alpha*T < 1 (p. 12), finite-T approximation (p. 17), exact MIP too slow (p. 26). Unstated: the tracking experiment samples from an estimated covariance (pp. 25-26); no MIP gap or reference value; no out-of-sample test. Future: consider shortfall in real-world environments (p. 27).

method_links.note: Risk measurement owned by financial economics is rewritten to stay in the LP class (sorting replaced by an LP), and a quadratic MIP is turned into a linear MIP.

Solver maturity drives the formulation (linear MIP codes available for decades, MIQP only recently). The argument is unquantified and points away from the newer class, the reverse of SW4's MIQO argument.
The MIP is stopped after five feasible solutions with no gap or bound, and 'either the best or very close to the best solution' is asserted without a number; a 2004 instance of Tension T1.

The baseline is the industry rule (mean-variance); the asset-allocation data were supplied by Chris Darnell and the work was partly funded by Merrill Lynch and General Motors. But judging is by in-sample frontiers, and the introduction's outperformance claim is not what Section 6.3 reports.
The 1999 Bertsimas-Popescu moment-bound device is reused with other coauthors in finance (Theorem 2).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The Table 1 bounds are 'best possible in the sense that there exist probability distributions that attain them'; the construction is not given in this paper.

transferable: Write the sum of the K smallest (or largest) of T values as the LP {sum z = K, 0 <= z <= 1} and dualize: 2^T subset constraints become n+T+1 variables and 2T+2 constraints (Theorem 3, pp. 15-16).

Express a tail functional through the quantile-regression check function, s_alpha(x) = (1/alpha) min_c E[rho_alpha(R'x - c)]. This gives convexity at once and a second route to the same LP (pp. 9-10, 16).
Motivate a new objective as the exact criterion of a dominance theorem for a whole utility class (Levy-Kroll), not as a modelling preference (pp. 4-5).
Tabulate model risk as the ratio of the distribution-free worst case to the parametric value, per risk level (Table 2: up to 3.7 at alpha = 1%, pp. 7-8).

Design synthetic assets the baseline cannot distinguish (same mean and standard deviation, zero correlation, skew via call and put overlays), so differences are attributable to the new criterion (p. 20).
Report allocations over 100 replications as median and 10%/90% bands against the risk-level knob (Figs. 1-5, pp. 19-24).

quotes.text: This formulation replaces sorting, usually required for computing quantile-based quantities, with an appropriately chosen linear program.
The reason for this is that running times for exact optimality can be excessive.

title: Solving convex programs by random walks
contribution: A randomized cutting-plane method that queries the average of random-walk samples of the current polytope solves convex feasibility and optimization with an oracle-optimal O(nL) separation-oracle calls. It extends to the intersection of a set given by a separation oracle and a centered set given by a membership oracle.
problem_entry: {CP; LO special case} Convex optimization with a separation oracle is the frontier of polynomial-time solvability (Ellipsoid, Vaidya). The entry imports random-walk sampling from volume computation and takes up the open case of a membership oracle combined with a separation oracle (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Query the sample mean of N random points of the enclosing polytope instead of Levin's intractable exact centroid. Every oracle cut then removes a constant fraction of the volume with high probability, so at most 2nL iterations are needed (pp. 2-3, 9-10).
assumptions: K is closed and bounded, inside a cube of width R, and if nonempty contains a cube of width r; L = log(R/r) (pp. 2-4). Separation oracle, or membership oracle with a known interior ball (p. 15). High probability means above any fixed constant (p. 9). Pairwise-independent samples suffice for Lemma 5 (p. 10). Technicalities of near-uniform, nearly independent sampling are set aside (p. 14). No data.
proof_devices: Theorem 3: Grunbaum's 1/e theorem generalized to 1/e - t for halfspaces through a point at distance t from the centroid (p. 6)

Lemma 4: the marginal density of an isotropic convex body is below 1, via Brunn-Minkowski symmetrization and moving mass away from the centroid (moment of inertia can only increase), reducing to a cone (pp. 6-8)
Lemma 5: E||z||^2 = n/N, so N = O(n) samples make every cut remove at least 1/3 of the volume (pp. 9-10)
Theorem 6: volume count, at most 2nL iterations, matching Vaidya and the Yudin-Nemirovski lower bound (pp. 3, 10)
Lemma 7 and Corollary 8: logconcave tails (Prekopa) plus a union bound over m constraints give N = O(log^2 m) for LPs (pp. 10-11)
Theorems 9-13: hit-and-run mixing, Rudelson's near-isotropy from O(n log^2 n) samples, O*(n^4) walk steps per iteration, multipoint walk by conductance comparison (pp. 12-15)
Theorem 14: membership plus separation oracles via a chain-of-bodies rounding (pp. 15-16)
Table I: total complexity O(nLT + n^7 L) against O(nLT + n^3.38 L) for Vaidya and O(n^2 LT + n^4 L) for the Ellipsoid method (p. 4)
experiments: none (no implementation; empirical evaluation called for, p. 16)
positioning: Simpler than the Ellipsoid/GLS and Vaidya methods; improves on the Ellipsoid method's O(n^2 L) oracle calls and matches Vaidya's O(nL) (p. 3). It calls the GLS membership algorithm intricate and concedes a higher total running time (pp. 1-2, 4, 15). Credits Kannan-Mount-Tayur 1995 and Levin's centroid idea (pp. 2-3).
writing: Three-sentence abstract with no theorem; an early comparison table that includes the losing rows (p. 4); proof intuitions in parentheses (p. 7); hedged forward-looking remarks on faster sampling (p. 4); ends on Extensions (p. 16).
limits_future: Higher arithmetic complexity than Vaidya (p. 4); sampling technicalities deferred to Kannan-Lovasz-Simonovits (p. 14); no experiments. Future: a sampling-based interior-point-like method, empirical evaluation, faster-mixing walks (p. 16).

method_links.note: Tractable in the 2004 complexity-class sense: an oracle-optimal count and polynomial time, with no solve times and an admitted higher running time. This is evidence for the drift recorded under Method 1's limitations, and an instance of the Taste warning 'polynomial time without solve times' that the authors flag themselves.
Levin's exact-centroid idea, labelled computationally intractable, becomes polynomial once random-walk sampling exists. The why-now is a tool change, unquantified and confined to a footnote.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: separation problem = nominal problem or oracle (GLS equivalence) as the tractability argument
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The whole method works in the separation/membership oracle model; recurs in S169 (p. 12) and S018 (pp. 7, 16-17, 20, 23).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: perturbation-robust version of a classical theorem so a sampled estimate suffices
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Grunbaum's 1/e is generalized to 1/e - t, so the sample mean can replace the exact centroid.

transferable: Generalize the classical lemma behind a method to an approximate version (Grunbaum 1/e to 1/e - t), so that sampling can replace an intractable exact computation (Theorem 3, p. 6).

Prove an extremal-body lemma by symmetrization plus the fact that moving mass away from the centroid can only increase the moment of inertia, reducing to a cone that can be computed (Lemma 4, Claim 1, pp. 6-8).
For polyhedra, union-bound over the m constraint hyperplanes the oracle can return: O(log^2 m) samples per iteration instead of O(n) (Lemma 7, Corollary 8, pp. 10-11).
Use only pairwise independence where a variance argument suffices, and discard the samples used to choose the query point to avoid correlation with later samples (pp. 10, 14).
Put a complexity table with the rows you lose next to the algorithm (Table I, p. 4).

quotes.text: Its complexity is optimal in terms of the number of oracle queries, but the overall running time can be higher than that of previous algorithms
The algorithms seems to merit empirical evaluation; in practice, it might be possible to sample more efficiently than the known worst-case bounds.

title: Probabilistic Combinatorial Optimization: Moments, Semidefinite Programming, and Asymptotic Bounds
contribution: Shows that the Meilijson-Nadas-type bound on the expected optimal value of a 0-1 problem with random objective coefficients is tight under any marginal moment information. The bound is computed by SDP in polynomial time whenever the nominal problem is polynomial (compactly when it has a compact LP) and applied to PERT tardiness, and exact asymptotic constants are derived for assignment, spanning tree and TSP without independence.
problem_entry: {CP+SD+IO; AP: PERT} Expected optimal values of random 0-1 problems are hard to evaluate, and classical analysis assumes independence. Since dependence would need exponentially many estimates, the paper optimizes over all dependence structures that match marginal moments, motivated by project completion times with unknown correlations (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: The sup-min interchange bound min_d {Z(d) + sum_i sup E[c_i - d_i]^+} is tight for any marginal moment information. Each inner problem is univariate and exactly an SDP, and the remaining constraint is separated by the nominal solver (pp. 6-12).
assumptions: Marginal moments of piecewise-polynomial functions with given supports, no cross moments, E|c_i| finite (pp. 2-3); interior moment vector for strong duality (p. 5); a polynomially solvable nominal problem (p. 12) or a compact LP hull (p. 13). Asymptotics: common continuous F without independence, equal-cardinality solutions, each element in equally many solutions, F(c) = rho c^alpha near 0 (pp. 17-19). The two-moment case adds a partition into disjoint solutions (pp. 22-23). Data: two Birge-Maddox PERT networks (pp. 15-17).
proof_devices: Isii duality for the moment problem over distributions (Theorem 2.1, p. 5)
Meilijson-Nadas inequality with an arbitrary vector d and the sup-min interchange (pp. 6-7)
Theorem 3.1: tightness via minimal univariate constants, whose sum is the minimal multivariate constant, then summing constraints over i in B_p and not in B_p (pp. 8-10)
Proposition 3.3: univariate polynomial nonnegativity on an interval is a PSD condition (Nesterov; Bertsimas-Popescu) (p. 11)
Theorem 3.4: polynomial time because the separation problem is the nominal problem with objective d, plus the GLS equivalence of separation and optimization (p. 12)
Theorem 3.5: a compact SDP by substituting the LP dual of a compact convex-hull description (pp. 12-13)
Theorem 5.1: KKT with uniform dual multipliers 1/P from symmetry gives a closed form (pp. 18-19); Theorem 5.3: scaling by explicit integrals (p. 20)
explicit moment-matching distribution (cyclic unions of disjoint feasible solutions) giving the trivial bound 0 under two moments (p. 23)
experiments: Two Birge-Maddox PERT networks (10 activities on 3 paths; 29 activities on 14 paths), five due dates each, SeDuMi 1.03 on a Pentium II 550 MHz, under a minute in total. Bound values are compared with the values reported in [5] (not rerun): tighter at every due date except one tie, and a third moment tightens further (Tables 4.2, 4.4, pp. 15-17). Asymptotic constants are compared with the independence literature (Tables 5.2-5.3, pp. 21-23). No simulation check and no failure reported.
positioning: Generalizes Meilijson-Nadas and Weiss and settles a tightness question left open in the PERT literature (pp. 2-3). Corrects Birge-Maddox as a consequence of the theorem ('a heuristic method', p. 16) and faults their linearization's lack of precision (p. 15). Cites Lasserre and Parrilo for SOS but avoids it (pp. 5, 10-11); places its constants beside the independence results (pp. 21-22).
writing: Contribution list (a)-(d) with the headline asymptotic table up front (pp. 3-4). The obstacle is stated plainly before the fix (pp. 4-5); max/min results come in pairs (pp. 10, 19). 'Conclusions and extensions' contains only a summary (p. 24).
limits_future: In the body only: the general formulation is exponential (pp. 4-5); compactness needs a compact LP (p. 13); the asymptotics exclude e.g. Steiner trees (p. 18); two moments give the trivial bound 0 (p. 23). Integrality of m in the construction is not discussed (p. 23). No future directions (p. 24).

method_links.note: A probabilistic-combinatorial quantity is written as a convex/semidefinite program that inherits the nominal class: polynomial when the nominal problem is (nominal solver as separator), compact when it has a compact LP. The boundary is printed for the direct multivariate dual.

Prices information rather than a property: the value of a third moment and the cost of dropping independence (0.5 against pi^2/6 for assignment). No knob, solution-independent bound or decision-maker framing.
The Bertsimas-Popescu device is carried to a new problem class with new coauthors, as S031 carries it into finance; SKILL.md lists Popescu and Natarajan in one CP lineage.

transferable: With marginal-only information, interchange sup and min and dualize each univariate inner problem separately. A hard multivariate positivity constraint becomes 2n univariate ones, each exactly SDP-representable (pp. 6-11).

Prove polynomial-time solvability of the uncertainty-aware 0-1 problem by showing that its separation problem is the nominal problem (GLS) (Theorem 3.4, p. 12). If the nominal problem has a compact LP, substitute its LP dual for a compact formulation (Theorem 3.5, pp. 12-13).
For symmetric families, set the dual multipliers uniform (1/P) and check KKT to get closed forms (Theorem 5.1, pp. 18-19).
Show the limit of a weak information model by an explicit distribution that matches the moments and makes the objective trivial (cyclic unions of disjoint feasible solutions, p. 23).
Rerun a competitor's published instances and report the value of one extra moment on the same instances (Tables 4.2 and 4.4, pp. 16-17).

quotes.text: Instead of trying to characterize this exact structure, we optimize over all dependent structures with the given marginal moment information.

The key observation is that although it is difficult to express exactly the nonnegativity of a multivariate polynomial, we can use positive semidefinite constraints to express the nonnegativity of a univariate polynomial over an interval.

title: Optimal inequalities in probability theory: A convex optimization approach
contribution: Formulates tight moment inequalities for P(X in S) as a primal-dual pair of conic programs. It solves the univariate case as one SDP, with closed forms for up to three moments; gives a convergent SDP hierarchy for the multivariate case; proves NP-hardness for k >= 2 on R^n_+ and k >= 4 on R^n; and gives polynomial algorithms for k = 1 and k = 2 over unions of convex sets.
problem_entry: {CP; SD} A question internal to probability theory: are the Markov, Chebyshev and Chernoff bounds best possible, how do they generalize, and is there an optimization theory for them? The gap is taken from critics of moment theory (Diaconis, Kemperman, Smith) (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: The tight bound is an LP over measures whose dual is an LP over polynomials g >= indicator of S on Omega. Univariate nonnegativity is exactly a PSD condition, so the univariate tight bound is one SDP, and Putinar's representation gives SDP relaxations in n dimensions (pp. 5-16).
assumptions: Random vector on Omega with given moments up to order k; S and Omega semialgebraic (pp. 2, 14-15). Complexity statements assume rational data, with efficiency polynomial in the data and log(1/epsilon) (p. 4). Strong duality needs an interior moment vector (p. 6); the hierarchy needs Putinar compactness (p. 14); the k = 2 case needs an invertible covariance (p. 20). No data.
proof_devices: primal LP over measures and dual LP over polynomials; weak duality (Theorem 2.1) and strong duality for interior moments (Theorem 2.2) (pp. 5-6)
Proposition 3.1: univariate nonnegativity on R via even-multiplicity root factorization into a sum of squares, extended to rays and intervals by rational substitutions (pp. 7-10)
Theorem 3.2: tight univariate bounds as single SDPs (pp. 10-12); Theorem 3.3 / Table 2: closed forms for k <= 3, proof deferred to Popescu's thesis (pp. 12-13)
Proposition 4.2 and Putinar's theorem: a convergent SDP hierarchy ZD(d), monotone in d, not polynomial-size in general (Theorem 4.3, Corollary 4.4, pp. 13-16)
Propositions 4.5-4.6: NP-hardness by reducing matrix copositivity to the separation problem, plus optimization-separation equivalence (pp. 16-17)
Theorem 5.1: the k = 1 bound via LP dual, scaling and minimax exchange, as n convex problems (pp. 17-18); Theorem 5.2: two-point extremal distributions and limiting sequences (pp. 19-20)
Algorithms A and B: separation by convex minimization over Omega and over S, with a PSD test first for k = 2 (pp. 20, 23)
Marshall-Olkin's k = 2 bound reread by gauge duality; a closed form by KKT when Gamma^{-1} M_delta >= 0 (pp. 21-22)
experiments: none (theorems, algorithms and closed-form tables only; Tables 1-2, pp. 5, 13)
positioning: A long history from Chebyshev-Markov to Karlin-Studden, Marshall-Olkin, Isii, Smith and Shapiro (pp. 3-4). Takes the duality theory as given and adds algorithms, complexity and closed forms; says Smith's procedure lacks a convergence proof and an efficiency study (p. 4). Credits Nesterov, Shor, Lasserre, Parrilo and Marshall-Olkin (pp. 7, 13, 20-21) and revives the 1937 Uspensky bound as strangely ignored (pp. 4, 23).
writing: Opens with three numbered questions (p. 1); critics' quotations define the gap (pp. 3-4); the contribution list is keyed to sections and closed by a landscape table (pp. 4-5). Negative results are announced as unsurprising (pp. 13, 16); the concluding remarks only summarize (pp. 23-24).
limits_future: Stated: no polynomial-size exact multivariate SDP in general (pp. 13, 16), NP-hardness thresholds (p. 17), the interior-moment requirement (p. 6). Implicit: no numerical illustration; the k = 3 proofs and an alternative k = 2 proof are in Popescu's thesis (pp. 12, 21); no procedure to extract an extremal distribution from the SDP (pp. 19-21). No future directions (pp. 23-24).

method_links.note: The clearest case: a central probability-theory problem is written exactly as a convex/semidefinite program, with a dual certificate and the boundary printed (NP-hard for k >= 2 on R^n_+ and k >= 4 on R^n).

Step 4 refined: the worst-case distribution is the primal (measure) optimum, built by hand for k = 1 and cited from Marshall-Olkin for k = 2. The SDP dual solution gives the bound certificate, not the distribution.

The why-now is a named critique of the old community (Diaconis, Kemperman, Smith), answered by modern convex/semidefinite optimization; unquantified. The old belief is partly confirmed by NP-hardness, so the boundary is mapped rather than the belief conceded or refuted.
Problem choice is internal to theory, with no owner, data or decision (applications only cited, p. 3). Taste mark 6 (problems and data first) does not describe this CP line (also S045).
[inferred, thin] Teachability appears after the fact, as a claim about textbooks, not as a stated pre-start gate.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tightness is defined as attainment, exact or asymptotic; extremal two-point distributions and limiting sequences are constructed for k = 1, and Marshall-Olkin's are cited for k = 2.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The whole (n, k, Omega) framework bounds probabilities over all distributions with the given moments.

transferable: Turn the question whether an inequality is best possible into an LP over measures with moment constraints and its dual over polynomials. Weak duality gives validity; strong duality (interior moment vector) gives tightness (pp. 5-6).
Univariate nonnegativity on an interval: reduce it to nonnegativity on R by a rational substitution, then to a PSD Gram matrix, so one lemma covers six cases (Prop. 3.1, pp. 7-10).
Build a convergent SDP hierarchy from Putinar's representation with a degree parameter d, and state that the size is not polynomial in general (Theorem 4.3, Corollary 4.4, pp. 15-16).
Prove NP-hardness of a bound problem by reducing matrix copositivity (COPOS) to its separation problem (Props. 4.5-4.6, p. 17).
Certify tightness by constructing extremal two-point distributions, with limiting sequences when the bound is not attained (Theorem 5.2, pp. 19-20).
Separation by two convex minimizations, over Omega for g >= 0 and over S for g >= 1, gives polynomial algorithms for unions of convex sets (Algorithms A and B, pp. 20, 23).
Summarize a problem family's solvable and NP-hard cases in a single landscape table (Table 1, p. 5).

quotes.text: In this paper, we formulate the problem of obtaining best possible bounds as an optimization problem and use modern optimization theory, in particular convex and semidefinite programming, to give concrete answers to the questions above.
It is fair to say that a thorough understanding of the algorithmic aspects and the complexity of the (n, k, Ω)-bound problem is still lacking.
